steps.tx: Reconstruction of head and neck oncological defects aims to restore oral competence, speech articulation, deglutition, and facial appearance. Microvascular **free tissue transfer** has become the gold standard, providing well-vascularised, uncompromised distant tissue outside the field of previous or planned postoperative radiotherapy.
steps.say: After cancer surgery the head and neck must eat, speak, swallow and face the world again. Free tissue transfer is the gold standard because it imports healthy distant tissue with its own blood supply, from well outside the zone that radiation has damaged or will damage.

nodes.label: Oncological resection and clear surgical margins
Defect analysis: mucosal, skeletal, or external skin loss
Microvascular free flap selection and microvascular anastomosis

steps.tx: The **radial forearm free flap** based on the radial artery and cephalic vein provides thin, exceptionally pliable, and hairless skin ideal for reconstructing oral tongue, floor of mouth, and pharyngeal defects. Allen test before surgery confirms adequate ulnar collateral circulation to the palmar arches.
steps.say: For the mobile tongue and floor of mouth, nothing beats the radial forearm flap: skin barely thicker than paper, perfectly pliable, and hairless. Before taking the radial artery, perform an Allen test to prove the ulnar artery alone can keep the hand alive.

vis.alt: Surgical blade handle for forearm flap elevation
vis.caption: Surgical instruments utilized in microvascular flap elevation. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: For mandibular defect reconstruction, the **fibula osteocutaneous free flap** based on the peroneal artery is the premier workhorse. It supplies up to 25 cm of dense bicortical bone suitable for multiple closing-wedge osteotomies and endosseous dental implants, while leaving 6 cm of distal fibula to preserve ankle stability.
steps.say: To rebuild a missing jaw, the fibula is king. Its peroneal artery feeds up to twenty-five centimetres of dense double-walled bone that can be wedge-cut into a new chin and later hold dental implants, while the lowest six centimetres stay behind so the ankle does not wobble.

right.title: Iliac Crest (DCIA)
points: Higher donor site abdominal wall morbidity

steps.tx: The **anterolateral thigh flap** or ALT provides immense versatility for massive head and neck composite defects, supplying extensive skin paddle dimensions and optional vascularised vastus lateralis muscle to obliterate radical neck dissection dead space and reliably protect exposed carotid vessels from salivary exposure.
steps.say: Huge composite defects need the anterolateral thigh flap, which brings an enormous skin paddle plus optional muscle from the vastus lateralis. That muscle bulk fills the hollow left by a radical neck dissection and drapes living tissue over the bare carotid, shielding it from saliva.

vis.alt: Closed suction surgical drain in neck reconstruction
vis.caption: Surgical drain placement to eliminate cervical dead space. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: The regional **pectoralis major myocutaneous flap** based on the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery remains the primary salvage flap when free tissue transfer fails or is contraindicated. It carries substantial muscle bulk to seal salivary fistulae and cover exposed major vessels in the neck.
steps.say: Keep the pectoralis major in reserve as the salvage flap. When a free flap fails or the patient cannot tolerate a long microsurgical case, this chest muscle swung up on its thoracoacromial vessels still seals salivary leaks and covers exposed neck vessels reliably.

right.title: Pectoralis Major Salvage
points: Excessive bulk in the oral cavity

steps.tx: Pharyngoesophageal defect reconstruction following total laryngopharyngectomy requires circumferential conduit restoration. The **free jejunal transfer** based on mesenteric vessels provides an active peristaltic, mucosal-lined tube with low fistula rates, though radial forearm flap tubed constructs and ALT flaps offer non-abdominal alternatives.
steps.say: After removing the whole larynx and pharynx, the throat must become a tube again. A short segment of jejunum on its mesenteric vessels makes a living peristaltic conduit lined with mucosa and leaks the least, though a tubed radial forearm flap spares the patient an abdominal operation.

rows: Avoids abdominal entry, resilient to radiation
Simple tubing geometry, minimal donor stenosis

steps.tx: Cervical recipient vessel selection is crucial for microvascular anastomotic success. The **facial artery** and superior thyroid artery are the most commonly utilized recipient arterial inflows, while the internal jugular vein end-to-side or external jugular vein end-to-end provide reliable low-pressure venous runoff.
steps.say: A perfect flap dies on bad plumbing, so choose recipient vessels well. The facial and superior thyroid arteries are the usual inflows, and for outflow the internal jugular vein joined end to side or the external jugular joined end to end both drain dependably.

nodes.label: Arterial inflow: facial artery or superior thyroid artery
Microvascular hand-sewn 9-0 nylon or coupler anastomosis
Venous outflow: internal jugular vein end-to-side

steps.tx: Salivary fistulae represent a major complication of head and neck reconstruction, increasing carotid blowout risks and prolonging hospitalisation. Prevention mandates water-tight two-layer mucosal insetting using **absorbable sutures**, wide vascularised muscle coverage between pharyngeal closures and great vessels, and continuous closed-suction drainage.
steps.say: The dreaded complication is a salivary fistula leaking onto the neck vessels, which can end in a carotid blowout. Prevent it with a watertight two-layer mucosal closure in absorbable suture, a blanket of vascularised muscle between the suture line and the great vessels, and closed suction drains.

rows: Muscle flap interposition, ligation of branch leaks
